title: Helping a Pupil Learn
scenario: You are teaching an English lesson in a primary school. The pupils are completing an exercise in which they choose the correct words to finish sentences. One pupil, Anna, is having difficulty with the task. Your goal is to help her understand the instructions, encourage her to participate and give constructive feedback.

steps.title: Noticing a Difficulty
opening: The pupils are working on a grammar exercise. They need to choose the correct verb forms to complete several sentences.
Most pupils have already started, but Anna is still looking at the example on the board.
You notice that she has not written anything yet. You want to check whether she understands what she needs to do.
steps.question: What would you say to Anna?

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Not yet. I'm not sure what to do.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks back at the example.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You realise that she needs another explanation.

choices.feedback: Readiness is not the same as understanding the task.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Not really. I don't understand the example.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna points to the sentence on the board.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You see that she needs help with the instructions.

choices.feedback: The question directly checks Anna’s comprehension.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: My book is already open.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks down at the exercise but does not begin working.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You notice that the problem is not her textbook but her understanding of the task.

choices.feedback: Her textbook is already open; the problem is understanding.

transition: You explain the exercise again, using a simpler example on the board.
Anna watches carefully. A few other pupils also look up from their books.
You decide to check the example with the class before everyone continues.

steps.title: Working Through an Example
opening: You write a short sentence on the board:
The pupils need to choose the correct verb form.
You want a volunteer to give the answer so that everyone can check their understanding of the example.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Most pupils remain quiet.

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: No questions.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: However, the correct answer has not been discussed yet.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the two verb forms and invite a pupil to answer.

choices.feedback: Asking about questions does not elicit an answer to the example.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Several pupils begin speaking at once.

reaction.speaker: some_pupils
reaction.text: Go!

reaction.speaker: other_pupils
reaction.text: Goes!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: The answers overlap, and it is difficult to tell who understands the rule.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You indicate that one pupil should answer at a time.

choices.feedback: A chorus makes it harder to identify whether an individual understands.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Maria raises her hand.

reaction.speaker: maria
reaction.text: Goes!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You nod and point to the completed sentence.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna looks at the example again.

choices.feedback: This invites a pupil to volunteer an answer to the example.

transition: You confirm that the correct answer is “goes” and briefly explain the rule.
Anna looks more confident. She begins working on the first sentence in her exercise.
A moment later, she raises her hand.

steps.title: Encouraging Participation
opening: Anna has chosen a word for the first sentence, but she seems uncertain about her answer.
You want to encourage Anna to attempt the answer without being afraid of making a mistake.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Okay, I'll try.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna looks at the sentence and gives her answer.

choices.feedback: This directly encourages Anna to attempt her answer.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Thank you.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She takes another moment to think.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: After a short pause, she gives her answer.

choices.feedback: Reassurance helps, but does not explicitly encourage an attempt.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna looks confused.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: But I haven't answered yet.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She hesitates, then looks at the sentence again.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You give her an opportunity to answer, and she makes an attempt.

choices.feedback: Rejecting an answer before it is given discourages participation.

transition: Anna gives her answer. She has chosen an incorrect verb form, although the rest of the sentence is correct.
You want to help her recognise that she is close to the correct answer and encourage her to try again.

openingMessages.speaker: anna
openingMessages.text: I think I know, but I'm not sure. Can I try?

steps.title: Correcting a Mistake
opening: Anna has completed the sentence, but one word is incorrect.
She looks towards you, waiting for feedback.
You want to show that her answer is close to being correct and explicitly encourage another attempt.
steps.question: What would you say?

choices.text: Good try, but not quite right.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Which part is wrong?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks at the sentence again.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You point to the verb, and she begins reconsidering her answer.

choices.feedback: This indicates an error, but does not explicitly invite another attempt.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna smiles at first, but then compares her sentence with the example on the board.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Wait, I think I made a mistake.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She checks the verb again and begins looking for the correct form.

choices.feedback: Confirming an incorrect answer gives misleading feedback.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Oh, I think I know!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks at the verb and tries a different form.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Her new answer is correct.

choices.feedback: This acknowledges that the answer is close and prompts a retry.

transition: Anna checks her answer once more and corrects the verb.
You look at the completed sentence. This time, everything is correct.
Anna turns towards you, waiting to hear whether she has succeeded.

steps.title: Recognising Success
opening: Anna has corrected her mistake successfully.
She looks pleased but still wants confirmation that her answer is correct.
You want to clearly acknowledge her successful result.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Thank you!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna smiles and looks back at her exercise.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She seems more confident about continuing.

choices.feedback: This clearly confirms and praises the correct result.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Is it completely correct now?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks at her sentence once more.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You nod to confirm that she has finished it correctly.

choices.feedback: This sounds as though the answer is only partly correct.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna looks disappointed.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Oh. What should I change?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She checks her sentence again.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You look at her answer and confirm that it is actually correct.

choices.feedback: This falsely rejects Anna’s correct answer.

transition: Anna understands that her corrected answer is right.
The other pupils are continuing the exercise. There are several more sentences to complete.
Anna has finished the first sentence and is ready to move on.

steps.title: Continuing Independently
opening: Anna looks at the next sentence in her book.
You want to support her independence and encourage her to continue with the exercise.
steps.question: What would you say?

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Okay!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna moves on to the next sentence and begins working independently.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks more confident than before.

choices.feedback: This encourages another independent attempt at the next sentence.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Thank you, teacher.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She takes a moment to read the next sentence carefully.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Then she begins working on it by herself.

choices.feedback: This is supportive but does not explicitly invite her to continue.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Anna stops looking at the exercise.

reaction.speaker: anna
reaction.text: Should I stop working?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: She looks towards you, waiting for clarification.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: You indicate that she should continue with the next sentence.

choices.feedback: This unnecessarily stops the exercise rather than supporting independence.

openingMessages.speaker: anna
openingMessages.text: I think I can do the next one myself.

final: Anna continues completing the exercise independently.
The other pupils are also working. You walk around the classroom, checking their progress and offering help where necessary.
The lesson continues in a calm, supportive atmosphere.
